issues.failure_explanation: With the paper's own conventions ($\Omega=\sum dq_i\wedge dp_i$, $\Omega(v_1,v_2)=v_1^TJ_{2n}v_2$, $J_{2n}=\begin{bmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{bmatrix}$), the Jacobian of the defined map is $DH=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\I&H_V\end{pmatrix}$ and direct computation gives $(DH)^TJ_{2n}(DH)=-J_{2n}$: the map is anti-symplectic, not symplectic (e.g. $V=0$, $\eta=0$ gives $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, which pulls $\Omega$ to $-\Omega$). The symplectic version requires $\hat y=-x+\nabla V(y)$, exactly the sign used in the nonlinear embedding of Section 3.2, so Definition def:Henon-map and eq:nonlinear-sym-lift are mutually sign-inconsistent. The claim that the Henon mapping itself preserves symplectic structure is therefore false as written. (The layer $[H]^4$ is nevertheless symplectic, since the composition of two anti-symplectic maps is symplectic, so HenonNet-level symplecticity claims survive.)

failure_location.quote: The fundamental building block is the H\'enon mapping, which enables intricate nonlinear transformations while preserving symplectic structure:

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either flip the sign in Definition def:Henon-map to $\hat y=-x+\nabla V(y)$ (adjusting the inverse formula in Proposition prop:added-1 accordingly), or keep the definition and correct the claim: the single Henon map is anti-symplectic with respect to $\Omega$, while the layer $[H]^4$, and hence HenonNets, are symplectic.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted symplecticity of the elementary Henon mapping is unreliable and Section 3.1's basic construction is inconsistent with Section 3.2's embedding sign. No labelled result is invalidated: Proposition prop:added-1's inverse formula is correct for the definition as stated, and HenonNet symplecticity survives via the fourth-power layer.
issues.title: Henon mapping as defined is anti-symplectic, contradicting the claimed symplecticity
issues.why_classification: A local sign/claim correction; under either repair the fourth-power layers remain exactly symplectic, so every architecture-level symplecticity claim and the ROM guarantees are preserved.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: This composite structure possesses universal approximation capability for symplectic embeddings, as formalized in the following theorem:

The universal approximation capability of H\'enonNets implies that any symplectic diffeomorphism, including the nonlinear embedding defined above, can be approximated arbitrarily closely by composing a fixed linear embedding with H\'enonNet transformations.

More critically, H\'enonNet has been proven to possess a universal approximation theorem for nonlinear symplectic mappings~\cite{turaev2002polynomial}, making it suitable for our symplectic model reduction framework.
This universal approximation result establishes that our composite architecture can approximate any symplectic embedding while maintaining exact symplectic structure preservation.

It is worth emphasizing again that the cotangent lift is an incomplete parameterization of $\mathrm{SpSt}(2k,2n)$, whereas the others offer complete parameterizations of the corresponding linear or non-linear symplectic embedding manifolds.

issues.failure_explanation: No proof or reference is given for Theorem thm:universal-approx. The only support invoked is the universal approximation of HenonNets for symplectic mappings $\mathbb{R}^{2n}\to\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ (same dimension), which cannot imply the stated approximation of symplectic embeddings $\mathbb{R}^{2k}\to\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with $k<n$: the source's own reduction calls the embedding $g:\mathbb{W}\to\mathbb{V}$ a 'symplectic diffeomorphism', a category error since domain and codomain have different dimensions. Approximating a general symplectic embedding $\Phi$ by $H\circ G\circ\iota$ requires at minimum that $\Phi$ be (approximately) the restriction of a symplectomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ to $\iota(\Omega)$, a nontrivial extension property never established and sensitive to the topology of the compact domain $\Omega$. The statement also speaks of 'parameters of $\iota$' although $\iota$ is elsewhere fixed and not learned (immaterial, since $G\iota$ already ranges over all of $\mathrm{SpSt}(2k,2n)$).

issues.overall_effect: The advertised 'universal approximation guarantees' of the composite embedding architecture, the justification for adopting the fixed canonical inclusion $\iota$ in eq:direct-henon-embed ('the practical equivalence due to universal approximation allows us to adopt a simpler, fixed embedding strategy'), and the Section 5 claim of 'complete parameterizations of ... non-linear symplectic embedding manifolds' are all unsupported. No labelled formal result depends on the theorem.
issues.title: Universal approximation theorem for symplectic embeddings is stated without proof and its invoked support does not apply
issues.why_classification: The theorem is a central advertised guarantee with no proof; its only invoked dependency is used outside its scope; every supported resolution either requires essentially new approximation arguments or abandons the advertised embedding-approximation guarantee, and the source supports no complete resolution.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: u_t(x,0) = -\omega u^{0}_x(x),
where $a_0\in [7,9]$, $x_0\in[-0.2,0.2]$, and $\omega$ represents the wave speed.
Notably, despite training only on data up to $t = 12$, the model successfully extrapolates to $t = 24$, demonstrating robust long-term prediction capability.

issues.failure_explanation: $u^0(x-\omega t)$ solves the Cauchy problem on the whole line with $u_t(x,0)=-\omega u_x^0$, but it is not the solution of the stated initial-boundary value problem: since $u^0$ is supported in $[\tfrac12+x_0-2/a_0,\ \tfrac12+x_0+2/a_0]\subset(0,1)$ and the wave travels right with speed $\omega=0.1$ ($\omega^2=0.01$), the profile reaches $x=1$ at $t\approx(\tfrac12-x_0-2/a_0)/\omega\in[0.14,4.8]$ (about $t\approx2$ for the displayed case $a_0=8.939$, $x_0=0.079$), after which $u(1,t)=u^0(1-\omega t)\neq0$, violating the Dirichlet condition; the true solution involves reflections throughout the training window $[0,12]$ and prediction horizon $[0,24]$. (The reference \eqref{eqn:linear1} also points at the spline definition rather than the PDE.)

failure_location.quote: The exact solution to \eqref{eqn:linear1} is \begin{equation} u(x,t ) =u^{0}(x-\omega t). \end{equation}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the exact-solution claim to times before the wave reaches the boundary, or replace it by the reflected (method-of-images) solution, or delete the claim.
issues.overall_effect: The analytic characterization of the Example 1 model problem is false; the benchmark description is unreliable (the snapshot data are generated by the Stormer-Verlet scheme, so no computational claim is directly invalidated).
issues.title: Claimed exact solution of the linear-wave IBVP violates the stated boundary conditions
issues.why_classification: One locally false analytic claim that is unused in the computations; correcting or removing it preserves every substantive and numerical claim of the example.

From the stated discrete Hamiltonian, $
abla_{\mathbf z}H=\Delta x\,\mathrm{diag}(-\omega^2D_{xx},I_N)\mathbf z$, so the asserted identity $
abla_{\mathbf z}H=L\mathbf z$ fails for the stated $L=\mathrm{diag}(I_N,\omega^2D_{xx})$: the blocks are swapped, the sign of the $D_{xx}$ block is wrong, and the $\Delta x$ scaling is missing (indeed $
abla_pH=\Delta x\,\mathbf p

Moreover $J_{2N}L\mathbf z=(\omega^2D_{xx}\mathbf p,-\mathbf q)$, which is neither the stated first-order system $(\mathbf p,\ \omega^2D_{xx}\mathbf q)$ nor Hamiltonian-consistent, since the indefinite $L$ is not the Hessian of the stated $H$ (with $D_{xx}$ negative definite it even produces exponentially growing modes).

The initial velocity $u_t(x,0)$, equivalently the initial momentum $p(x,0)$ required by the canonical formulation, the discrete Hamiltonian, and the Stormer-Verlet snapshot generation, is never specified anywhere in Example 2 (contrast Example 1, which specifies $u_t(x,0)=-\omega u_x^0$). The full-order problem and the data-generation procedure are therefore not well-defined from the source.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We consider periodic boundary conditions; i.e., $x$ belongs to a one-dimensional torus of length $L$.
When $\epsilon=1$, $|u(x,t)|$ forms a solitary wave propagating with speed $c$; for other values, the solution consists of interacting solitary waves moving bidirectionally~\cite{sulem2007nonlinear}.

issues.failure_explanation: The phase $c(x-x_0)/x$ is singular at $x=0$, which is a point of the torus of length $L$ (coordinates are taken modulo $L$), and it is not periodic ($u_0$ has no well-defined value at $x\equiv0$ and the values near $0$ and $L$ do not match), so the stated initial condition does not define a function on the stated domain. Moreover, a bright soliton of speed $c$ for this normalization requires a linear phase ( $e^{ic(x-x_0)/2}$ with amplitude $\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{sech}(x-x_0)$ for $\epsilon=1$ ); with the stated nonlinear phase the claimed solitary-wave behavior fails for this initial condition.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the phase by a well-defined periodic one, e.g. $\exp(ic(x-x_0)/2)$ (the standard soliton phase for speed $c$), and specify $x_0$.
issues.overall_effect: The initial data of Example 3 are ill-defined as written and inconsistent with the stated soliton benchmark; the example's setup cannot be reproduced from the source.
issues.title: Schrodinger-example initial condition is ill-defined on the torus (singular, non-periodic phase)
issues.why_classification: Local correction of the initial-condition formula; the example's claims survive.

\dot{\mathbf{x}} = J_{2n}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}H(\mathbf{x}).

issues.failure_explanation: Under the paper's own Hamilton convention $\dot{\mathbf x}=J\nabla H$ (eq:hamilton-compact), the stated $H_{\rm cont}$ yields $q_t=-2p_{xx}+2\epsilon(q^2+p^2)p$ and $p_t=2q_{xx}+2\epsilon(q^2+p^2)q$, which disagrees in signs and factors with eq:schro-can; no sign convention repairs it, since the kinetic and nonlinear terms must enter with opposite signs: the Hamiltonian generating eq:schro-can is $\int(\tfrac{\epsilon}{4}(q^2+p^2)^2-\tfrac{q_x^2+p_x^2}{2})dx$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \frac{d}{d t} \mathbf{z}=\bbJ_{2 N} \nabla_{\bf z} H({\bf z})=\bbJ_{2 N} L\mathbf{z} + \bbJ_{2 N}\mathbf{g}(\bf z),
q_{t}=p_{xx}+\epsilon (q^2+p^2)p \\ p_{t}=-q_{xx} -\epsilon(q^2+p^2)q
Snapshot data are generated by uniformly sampling 500 parameter values $\{\epsilon_i\}_{i=1}^{500}\subset[0.9,1.1]$, integrated numerically over $[0,20]$.

issues.failure_explanation: The stated $\mathbf g=((q_i^2+p_i^2)q_i,\ (q_i^2+p_i^2)p_i)$ carries no factor $\epsilon$, so the semi-discrete system $\dot{\mathbf z}=J_{2N}(L\mathbf z+\mathbf g)$ is not a discretization of eq:schro-can (whose nonlinearity is $\epsilon(q^2+p^2)p$ and $\epsilon(q^2+p^2)q$) and is completely independent of the parameter $\epsilon\in[0.9,1.1]$ on which the example's parametric snapshot generation is based.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Include the factor $\epsilon$ in $\mathbf g$, i.e. $\mathbf g=\epsilon\,((q_i^2+p_i^2)q_i,\ (q_i^2+p_i^2)p_i)$.
issues.overall_effect: The stated semi-discrete model of Example 3 does not correspond to the stated PDE and cannot represent the parametric dependence that defines the experiment.
issues.title: Nonlinear term g of the semi-discrete Schrodinger system omits the parameter epsilon
issues.why_classification: Local insertion of a missing factor; the example's claims survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \frac{d}{d t} \mathbf{z}=\bbJ_{2 N} \nabla_{\bf z} H({\bf z})=\bbJ_{2 N} L\mathbf{z} + \bbJ_{2 N}\mathbf{g}(\bf z),
Because the semi-discrete Hamiltonian is nonlinear, the St{\"o}rmer--Verlet time integrator must be applied in its implicit form.
H_{\rm cont}(q,p) = \int_0^L(q_x^2+p_x^2)+\epsilon/2(q^2+p^2)^2dx

issues.failure_explanation: For the displayed system, the Hamiltonian must satisfy $\nabla_{\mathbf z}H=L\mathbf z+\mathbf g(\mathbf z)$, i.e. $\partial H/\partial q_j=(D_{xx}\mathbf q)_j+(q_j^2+p_j^2)q_j$ (up to scaling). The gradient of the stated formula instead contains quartic terms, since $(q_{i-1}q_i-q_i^2)^2=q_i^2(q_{i-1}-q_i)^2$ is quartic rather than a quadratic difference (e.g. $\partial H/\partial q_j\sim\tfrac{2}{\Delta x}[q_j(q_{j-1}-q_j)(q_{j-1}-2q_j)+q_{j+1}^2(q_j-q_{j+1})]+\tfrac{\epsilon\Delta x}{2}q_j$), and the nonlinear term $\tfrac{\epsilon}{4}(p_i^2+q_i^2)$ is quadratic rather than quartic. The stated $H$ is thus neither the Hamiltonian of the stated semi-discrete system nor a discretization of the stated continuous Hamiltonian, although the reference data are claimed to be generated by applying implicit Stormer-Verlet to it.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Rewrite the discrete Hamiltonian as the Hamiltonian of the (epsilon-corrected) semi-discrete system, e.g. $H=\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}(\mathbf q^TD_{xx}\mathbf q+\mathbf p^TD_{xx}\mathbf p)+\tfrac{\epsilon\Delta x}{4}\sum_i(q_i^2+p_i^2)^2$ (quadratic difference terms, quartic nonlinearity), so that $\nabla_{\mathbf z}H=L\mathbf z+\mathbf g$.
issues.overall_effect: The semi-discrete formulation and the described reference-data generation of Example 3 are internally inconsistent; the full-order model of the example cannot be reconstructed from the source as stated.
issues.title: Discrete Hamiltonian of Example 3 is not the Hamiltonian of the stated semi-discrete system
issues.why_classification: Local rewrite of one displayed formula using the standard NLS discretization; no advertised theorem, rate, or guarantee is lost.
